procedural_history.originating_court: This case originated as Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 148 of 1983 directly in the Supreme Court under its Original Jurisdiction.
procedural_history.impugned_order: There is no mention of a lower court order being challenged. The case originated in the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There were no High Court proceedings as the case originated in the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court initially issued a writ of habeas corpus to respondents 1, 2, and 4, commanding them to produce C. Daniel and C. Paul before the Court on Dec. 12, 1983, and file a return. The matter was adjourned twice at the request of the Attorney General to allow the respondents to locate the two individuals. After a CBI enquiry failed to locate the individuals, the Court, on April 19, 1984, directed respondents 1 and 2 to pay exemplary costs of Rs. 1 lac each to the wives of the missing men as compensation for the torture, agony, and mental oppression they had suffered.

issue.issue_text: Whether the failure to produce the missing persons in respect of whom a writ of habeas corpus is issued, and to file a return, constitutes non-compliance with the mandatory direction of the writ.

facts: The Supreme Court issued a writ of habeas corpus to respondents 1, 2, and 4, commanding them to produce two missing persons (C. Daniel and C. Paul) before the Court on a specific date.
The writ also directed the respondents to file a formal return.
The respondents were served with the writ but failed to produce the two missing persons.
The respondents also failed to file the return as mandated by law.
law: When a writ of habeas corpus is issued, the person to whom it is directed is under a mandatory legal obligation to produce the body of the person alleged to be unlawfully detained before the Court on the specified day.
The person to whom the writ is directed is also legally obligated to make a formal return to the writ.
application: The Court noted that a writ of habeas corpus had been issued and served on the respondents.
It then observed that the respondents had failed to fulfill their legal obligations under the writ because they did not produce the missing persons and did not file the required return.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the respondents' failure to produce the missing persons and to file a return constituted non-compliance with the mandatory direction of the writ of habeas corpus.

issue.issue_text: What is the appropriate mode of enforcing obedience to a writ of habeas corpus when the authorities fail to produce the person.

facts: A writ of habeas corpus was issued and served on the respondents, directing them to produce two missing persons.
The respondents failed to produce the individuals and also failed to file a formal return to the writ as legally required.
law: A person to whom a writ of habeas corpus is directed is under a legal obligation to produce the body of the person allegedly detained and to make a formal return to the writ.
Wilful disobedience to a writ issued by a court constitutes civil contempt.
The appropriate mode of enforcing obedience to a writ of habeas corpus is by committal for contempt.
application: The Court noted that the respondents had failed to comply with the mandatory directions of the writ by not producing the missing persons and not filing a return.
The Court identified this failure as a wilful disobedience of its order, which constitutes civil contempt.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the appropriate mode of enforcing obedience to a writ of habeas corpus, when authorities fail to produce the person, is by committal for contempt.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the failure to produce the missing persons in respect of whom a writ of habeas corpus is issued, and to file a return, constitutes non-compliance with the mandatory direction of the writ.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner's argument, as affirmed by the court, was that the respondents' failure to produce the two missing persons constituted non-compliance. The petitioner implicitly argued that the respondents' explanation—that the men had left the army camp—was a false and distorted version of the facts designed to mislead the court and avoid responsibility for their disappearance.
respondent_arguments: The respondents asserted that they could not produce the two individuals, C. Daniel and C. Paul, because they had left the Phungref camp where the 21st Sikh Regiment was stationed. They supported this by stating that inquiries, including by the CBI, had been made but yielded no results in locating the two persons.

arguments.issue_text: What is the appropriate mode of enforcing obedience to a writ of habeas corpus when the authorities fail to produce the person.
appellant_arguments: The text does not specify the petitioner's proposed remedy. However, by pursuing the matter after the respondents failed to produce the individuals, the petitioner implicitly argued for a substantive enforcement action beyond merely accepting the respondents' claim that the persons could not be found.
respondent_arguments: The respondents, through the Attorney General, argued for the matter to be repeatedly adjourned to allow them more time to 'trace or locate the two persons'. Their proposed mode of enforcement was to continue the search, despite it having yielded no results.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In compliance with the mandatory direction contained in the Writ of Habeas Corpus, the person to whom it is directed is under a legal obligation to produce the body of the person alleged to be unlawfully detained before the Court on the day specified and to make a formal return to the writ.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The respondents committed civil contempt through their willful disobedience to the writ of habeas corpus by failing to produce the two missing persons and file a return. The court rejected the respondents' request for more time to search as 'shutting the eyes to the reality,' and drew the 'only possible inference' that the two men had met an unnatural death, for which the Union of India could not disown responsibility. As a remedy, the court ordered the payment of exemplary costs to the wives of the missing men.
legal_tests_applied: A writ of habeas corpus contains a mandatory direction requiring the person to whom it is directed to be under a legal obligation to produce the body of the person alleged to be unlawfully detained before the Court on the day specified and to make a formal return to the writ.
Civil contempt, defined as 'wilful disobedience to any judgment,' is established by the failure to comply with the mandatory directions of a writ of habeas corpus.

In cases of civil contempt, the court has the discretion to impose punishment including imprisonment, fines, or ordering the contemnor to pay costs, which can be awarded as 'exemplary costs' in appropriate circumstances.
why_respondent_won: The respondents failed to comply with the mandatory legal obligation of a writ of habeas corpus, which required them to produce the missing persons and file a formal return. The court found 'there has been failure to produce the missing persons in respect of whom writ is issued and to file the return as mandated by law.'
The respondents' failure was determined to be 'wilful disobedience to the writ,' which constitutes civil contempt.
The court rejected the respondents' request for more time to search, stating that to grant it 'is to shut the eyes to the reality.'

The court drew the 'only possible inference' from the circumstances that the missing persons 'must have met an unnatural death,' concluding that 'the Union of India cannot disown the responsibility in this behalf.'
policy_considerations: The court fashioned a remedy based on the suffering of the victims' families, choosing not to impose imprisonment or a fine but instead awarding monetary compensation 'keeping in view the torture, the agony and the mental oppression through which' the wives of the missing men had to pass.

The court utilized its power to award 'exemplary costs' as a permissible measure to enforce the writ and provide a remedy in a case where the state failed to comply with a court order and was held responsible for the disappearance of citizens.
